issues.legal_issue: A Hindu deity that represents a donor’s religious purpose may hold dedicated property and be taxed through the shebaits who possess and manage it.
material_facts: A will dedicated property to two Hindu deities and provided for the use of its income.
The will appointed shebaits, who were entrusted with possession and management of the dedicated property.
The income from the property was assessed on the deities through the shebaits.
issues.conclusion: A Hindu deity is a juristic entity capable of holding dedicated property and being taxed through its shebaits; the assessments did not require the shebaits to be assessed under section 41.
issues.legal_principle: A Hindu idol, as the legal person representing the donor’s religious purpose, may own dedicated property in the legal sense, with its possession and management entrusted to shebaits. The Court relied on Manohar Ganesh v. Lakshmiram, Vidyapurna Tirtha Swami v. Vidvanidhi Tirtha Swami, Maharanee Shibessouree Dehia v. Mothocrapath Acharjo, Prosanna Kumari Debya v. Golab Chand Baboo, Pramatha Nath Mullick v. Pradyumna Kumar Mullick, and Bhupati v. Ramlal.

predicates.income_tax_assessment_proceeding: The matter concerns an assessment of income for tax purposes.
predicates.dedicated_property_represents_religious_: Property was dedicated to a deity to serve a religious purpose identified by the donor.
predicates.shebaits_manage_dedicated_property: Shebaits were entrusted with possession and management of the dedicated property.

issues.definition: When an income-tax assessment concerns property dedicated to a deity for a religious purpose and managed by shebaits, the deity may be taxed through those shebaits.

issues.legal_issue: A Hindu deity is an individual within the meaning of the income-tax law’s category of taxable units.
material_facts: The tax authority assessed the deities as individuals on income from property dedicated to them.
The deities were treated in law as juristic entities capable of holding property.
The applicable tax law imposed tax on the income of specified taxable units, and its definition of individual did not expressly exclude artificial juridical persons.
issues.conclusion: A Hindu deity falls within the meaning of individual and may be treated as a unit of assessment.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922 includes artificial juridical persons within individual; sections 2(9) and 3 were considered alongside section 2(31) of the Income-tax Act, 1961. The Court relied on Commissioner of Income-tax v. Sodra Devi for the breadth of individual and on Cape Brandy Syndicate v. I.R.C. and Attorney General v. Clarkson for using later legislation to clarify an earlier ambiguous enactment. The Court also relied on the authorities establishing the juristic status of Hindu idols, including Manohar Ganesh v. Lakshmiram and Pramatha Nath Mullick v. Pradyumna Kumar Mullick.

predicates.income_tax_assessment_proceeding: The matter concerns an assessment of income for tax purposes.
predicates.assessed_entity_is_artificial_juridical_: The entity assessed is recognized in law as an artificial juridical person.
predicates.tax_law_charges_income_of_taxable_units: The applicable tax law imposes tax on income of entities within its taxable-unit categories.

issues.definition: In an income-tax assessment, an artificial juridical person assessed under a law charging income of taxable units falls within the individual category of taxable units.
